questions.question: Why can `Pressable`'s `style` prop be a function instead of a plain object?
options: It's just a stylistic alternative with no functional purpose
The function receives the current pressed state, letting you apply conditional styles (like reduced opacity) without manually tracking press state with useState
Function styles are required for performance reasons
Only function styles work with StyleSheet.create
questions.explanation: Pressable passes { pressed } into style and children functions, which is how you get press-feedback styling without wiring up your own onPressIn/onPressOut state.

questions.question: Why does the React Native team recommend `Pressable` over `TouchableOpacity`/`TouchableHighlight` for new code?
options: The older Touchable components have been completely removed
Pressable unifies their capabilities and adds finer-grained control over different press states
TouchableOpacity doesn't support onPress at all
There is no actual recommendation, they are fully interchangeable with no trade-offs
questions.explanation: Pressable is the newer, more capable API; the older Touchable components still work and appear in many codebases/libraries but are considered legacy for new development.

questions.question: Why does the card shadow example use `Platform.select({ ios: ..., android: ... })` instead of one shared style?
options: iOS and Android use completely different APIs for drop shadows — shadow* properties on iOS vs elevation on Android
Platform.select is required for every style object
Android doesn't support shadows under any circumstances
It's purely a code style preference with no functional need
questions.explanation: Shadow rendering is one of the areas where iOS and Android diverge at the native level, so a single cross-platform style property doesn't exist — Platform.select picks the right implementation per OS.

questions.question: What does naming two files `Header.ios.js` and `Header.android.js` achieve, compared to a single file with `Platform.OS` checks?
options: Nothing different — it's purely a naming convention with no effect on bundling
Metro (the bundler) automatically picks the matching file at import time based on the running platform, avoiding in-file branching for substantially different implementations
It disables the component on whichever platform's file is missing
It's required syntax whenever Platform.OS is used anywhere in the app
questions.explanation: The .ios.js/.android.js extension convention is resolved automatically by the bundler, which is cleaner than Platform.OS branching when two platform implementations are different enough to warrant separate files entirely.
